meta.title: What VCs Really Think About Personal AI Agents | E2347
meta.speakers: Deedy Das (Menlo Ventures, guest host), Kanu Gulati (Khosla Ventures), Chris Farmer (SignalFire), Shiel Mohnot (Better Tomorrow Ventures), Lon Harris (host)
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · AI math and science · startups vs labs · data companies · personal agents · founders and SaaS · investing in rivals

snapshot: A four-VC roundtable opens on **OpenAI's new math result**: with the earlier Navier-Stokes work, AI has made progress on four of the six unsolved Millennium Prize problems.
The panel's answer to 'what is left for startups?': **formalize messy domains, own proprietary vertical data, and run physical-world loops** (wet labs, robots, sensors) that labs won't prioritize.
Compute is seen as a bottleneck for **roughly the next 2-3 years**, not 5-7; after that lab capacity, trials and manufacturing become the constraint.

RL-environment and data companies are growing explosively but the panel splits on terminal value; **two of four have passed on the category**, and gross profit, concentration and durability are the open questions.

On personal agents, a **$10B-valued consumer agent startup** meets skepticism: incumbents hold distribution, trust, payments and ads; the category is large, but data-access fear and agent fatigue are real.
Founder profile is shifting to young, 'AI-pilled' builders running **thousands of agents with tiny teams**; meanwhile top-down SaaS faces seat-pricing and switching-cost erosion.
The Factory vs Cognition spat reopens the question of **funds backing competing companies**; the panel's answer is Chinese walls and accepting that pivots create overlap.

themes.title: AI math breakthroughs push investors toward formalization, wet labs and physical AI
themes.lead: The panel treats math as the first verifiable proof that AI can invent, and invests where results must still be formalized, tested or manufactured.
bullets: Deedy Das's framing: of seven Millennium Prize problems, one was solved 20+ years ago; OpenAI's new result plus its earlier Navier-Stokes work means progress on **four of the six** remaining.
Math is first because it is easy to verify; the extrapolation is to chemistry, physics and biology, making invention itself cheaper.
Kanu Gulati's bets formalize messy domains so AI can build proofs on proofs: one startup targeting taxes, another (Logos Research, from Imperial College) targeting financial code.
Biology angle: capture failed experiments too, not just clinical-trial successes, so models learn from them; breakthroughs on the brain, cancers and 'planetary health' are expected.
Limits: an AI-designed cancer therapy still needs safe-in-humans proof, and a better battery chemistry still needs manufacturing and testing, which is why physical AI is attracting money.
One panelist: a molecule costing $50M today may cost thousands in a few years, shifting the constraint to lab capacity, trials, manufacturing and patents.
themes.watch: Kanu Gulati says Khosla Ventures are 'very proud early investors in OpenAI', and admits the pace makes her 'uneasy'.

names.blurb: Source of the new math result; Khosla Ventures is an early investor.

themes.title: Can startups beat labs with 5,000 GPUs? Context, vertical data and new architectures
themes.lead: Deedy asked how startups compete when labs commit billions to compute; the panel's answer is that intelligence is an input and context, permissions and proprietary data are the product.
bullets: Deedy's challenge: labs run hundreds of thousands of GPUs against a startup's 5,000-10,000, and get the best revenue per incremental compute dollar.
Panelist: frontier-deployed engineers exist because enterprises need change management, guard rails and trust; one fund flipped from ~80% horizontal SaaS to ~80% **vertical AI** for data density.
Examples: a personal-injury-law AI player seen as dominant because 99% of its negotiation data is private, and a clinical-grade wearable with personal bio context.

Kanu: models are very inefficient in training data, training compute and serving; 1M-token context may become 100M, and lack of HBM is already driving open-lab innovation. Windborne's in-situ atmospheric data is her physical-world flywheel example.
She does not believe scaling or transformers alone reach AGI; compute constraints likely bind for the next 2-3 years, not 5-7.
Enterprise shift cited from Vercel data: proprietary to open-weight models went from roughly 80/20 to 20/80 in a matter of months.

quote.text: I'm not at all a believer that the models are just going to own everything.

themes.status: FASTEST 0 TO $1B REVENUE RUN-RATE, PER A TWEET
themes.title: RL-environment and data companies: explosive revenue, unclear terminal value
themes.lead: A tweet says the fastest company to $1B run-rate revenue is a data company, and the panel splits on whether those businesses last.
bullets: Deedy cited Gokul's tweet and noted most such revenue is non-recurring, margins vary, and investors disagree on whether to touch the category.
For: a panelist's fund backs Micro1 and sees the work moving from labs to enterprises as open-weight adoption rises; expects some demand to 'come back down' as fast as it rose.
Against: Kanu says labs eventually don't need the data, open-weight models can distill from top labs, so her fund has avoided the category.
Shiel Mohnot: look at gross profit, not headline revenue; customer concentration, structural vs temporary demand and little proprietary IP are open questions, but little fixed capital is needed.
Everyone agrees founder quality decides these deals; Shiel hasn't invested in any.
themes.watch: One panelist's fund is an investor in Micro1 and argues for the category.

names.name: Micro1
names.blurb: Training/RL data company; a panelist's fund is an investor.

themes.title: Personal agents: big category, but a $10B entry price faces incumbents
themes.lead: The panel thinks personal agents could be a major interface, but many doubt a startup beats Meta, Google, OpenAI or Apple on distribution, trust and monetization.
bullets: A $10B-valued consumer-agent startup (captions render its name 'Instinct'; not identified here) and Meta's 'Muse' agent drew questions from hedge-fund friends of Deedy: why fund it for $10B when it doesn't make money?

Bear case: only so many entry points into private data (Gmail holds SSNs, taxes); Facebook has ~3.5B users and Google ~4B, plus ads, wallets and commercial networks; startups would also need ads, hardware and payments.

Bull case: hundreds of millions of daily users plausible; one user got a €600 flight-delay refund handled end-to-end, paid a medical bill, and split bachelor-party costs instead of Splitwise; the winner needs only to be a top consumer interface.
Fatigue and security: Hark launched the day before, Sesame has a product, and another panelist reports agent fatigue; an agent reportedly posted bank details in a company Slack.
Kanu has avoided sharing card or SSN data; she wants an agent for phone calls (booking a child's party) and notes Rabbit, her early bet, 'promised too much' but described this world.
Fintech view: frictionless agents let users move debt or bank deposits quickly, pressuring rates and fee-based business models; a viral post imagined an agent-driven bank run.
Agents search differently: they visit hundreds of links where humans read one or two pages, so sites and businesses must be rebuilt for agent traffic.

themes.title: New founder class and the squeeze on top-down SaaS
themes.lead: Small teams running agents are changing what a good founder looks like, while seat-based SaaS loses growth physics and switching costs.
bullets: Deedy: teams of five run thousands of agents; panel agrees vision, selling and recruiting are evergreen, but a young cohort scales in accounting and legal without domain backgrounds.
Kanu: a chip-design startup plans a chip with ~20 people; 'AI-pilled' bets on frontier-model capability are an important axis, at any age.
One investor sees the median getting slightly worse and the extremes much stronger, e.g. a 19-year-old running ~50 agents to find website bugs and collect bounties.
Fund approaches: back deep domain experts and also 'heat-seeking missile' hackers; cloud-era cheapness is repeating with AI tools.
SaaS: traditional growth is 3x, 3x, 2x, 2x, 2x (per GC's Hemant, via Deedy); consumption-priced AI grows faster and sales talent leaves.

AI moves vendors from tech budgets to the labor layer, an order of magnitude bigger, so vertical beats horizontal; a panelist calls some SaaS 'cigar butt' businesses as seat pricing shrinks and agents handle migration.
Bending Spoons buys SaaS names (Airtable cited), cutting costs and raising prices; Figma is cited as still delivering strong numbers; compression also reflects ending zero-rate multiples.

quote.text: Switching costs have gone away. It's just so easy to switch from one product to another because AI can do the switching for you.

themes.status: FACTORY VS COGNITION SPAT, LAST WEEK
themes.title: Funds backing rivals: Factory vs Cognition and the AI co-opetition web
themes.lead: A public founder spat reopened whether VCs should fund competitors; the panel says pivots make overlap inevitable and Chinese walls manage it.
bullets: Spat: a Factory board-related incident led to posts from Factory's CEO Matan and Cognition's founder Scott, and Vinod Khosla calling Factory second-tier despite Khosla being a Factory investor.
Menlo invested in Factory that same week; Deedy says that decision predated the news and that both companies are great.
Kanu: multi-stage funds now often hold rivals; her firm uses a Chinese wall between partners; Shiel says his fund doesn't at the outset but has had portfolio pivots into rivalry.
Examples: Microsoft and OpenAI, Nvidia selling to labs while competing on open-weight models, clouds competing on chips.
A model-agnostic assistant product (name garbled) will use whichever frontier model is best, and xAI's data-center capacity was leased in a tens-of-billions deal to Anthropic.

takeaways.title: Look for startups that formalize messy domains or close the loop with wet-lab and robot experiments.
Test any vertical AI pitch for proprietary data that labs can't see; that is the defensibility the panel cites.
Judge RL-data companies on gross profit and customer concentration, not headline revenue.
Treat personal-agent startups skeptically against incumbent distribution, ads and payments unless they own a narrow domain.
Reprice seat-based SaaS for shrinking seats and zero switching cost; favor labor-layer AI.
If funding rivals, set Chinese walls and tell founders upfront.

hot_takes.take: I'm not at all a believer that the models are just going to own everything.
I don't believe that just scaling up will be the only way for us to continue winning the ultimate challenge for the next couple of years.
I think some of these businesses are literally cigar butt businesses.
I personally think that the large companies have a huge benefit here.

claims.claim: Compute and other component constraints persist for roughly the next 2-3 years, not 5-7.
Robotics sold in the US must source or license 65% of the bill of materials from US-friendly sources, rising to 75% next year.
AI has made major progress on four of the six remaining Millennium Prize problems.

other_news.title: Research habits: Kanu Gulati spends time with university professors and factory customers; Chris Farmer runs a 'listening tour' of labs, customers and regulators; Shiel Mohnot builds fintech theses (accounting) and says seed rounds now reach $100M+ valuations; Deedy Das plays with products to cut jargon.
Chris Farmer expects physical AI to draw a visceral, political backlash: people can throw a beer bottle at a humanoid robot or a Waymo in a way they can't at a chatbot.
Sources referenced: Gokul's tweet on data-company revenue, Vercel's open-weight data, GC's Hemant on SaaS growth physics, a viral banker post on agent-driven bank runs.
